title: Map key: how power and movement are drawn
intro: A short preview of the map styles the later chapters will use. Before borders were surveyed, the region held kingdoms, walled city-states, trading networks, a caliphate of emirates and many self-governing communities, and each is drawn its own way rather than as coloured land. Trade, migration and war each move differently too. Every example is real and cited, but this is a key, not a story: the full chapters will add more places and checks.

features.name: Bilma (Kawar oases)
features.what: An oasis town where rock salt was mined for the caravan trade. Salt is still produced in its natron pans today.

features.name: Kanem
features.what: A kingdom whose heartland lay north-east of Lake Chad. It controlled trade routes to the north and exported salt, ivory, slaves and animal products.
features.location: Rough. Kanem's first capital, probably Njimi, has never been located, so the marker sits at Mao, the main town of today's Kanem region of Chad, with a ring for the uncertainty.
features.disputed: Kanem's founding is usually dated to about 700 CE, but some sources give about 600 or about 900.

features.name: Salt road from Bilma to Kanem
features.what: Caravans carried rock salt south from Bilma to the savanna north of Lake Chad, and slaves and ivory went north in exchange. It was the shortest crossing of the Sahara, part of the road from Tripoli by way of Murzuk.
features.location: A line between the two places. The caravans' track across the dunes is not drawn.

features.name: Daura
features.what: Remembered as the mother city of the Hausa states.
features.location: Today's town of the same name.

features.name: Katsina
features.label: left
features.what: A Hausa state around a walled city, believed to have been founded about 1100. By the 15th century it was a trading centre.
features.location: Today's walled city of the same name.

features.name: Kano
features.what: A Hausa state around a walled city. By the Kano Chronicle's dating its walls were begun under Gijimasu (1095 to 1134).
features.evidence: Secondary sources; the Kano Chronicle's early dates are reconstructions

features.name: Ngazargamu (Bornu)
features.what: Founded about 1472 as the first substantial capital of Bornu, the kingdom that grew from Kanem, in the fork of two rivers near today's Geidam. It was captured and destroyed in 1808.

features.name: Kano's tribute to Bornu
features.what: Bornu was recognised as Kano's overlord and paid tribute.
features.disputed: One source says Bornu made the Hausa states its vassals in the 15th century, with tribute sent through Daura, but is unsure whether this covered all of them or only Kano and Biram. Another names only Kano.

features.name: Fulani moving into Hausaland and Bornu
features.period: by the 15th century, then into Bornu
features.what: By the 15th century there was a steady flow of Fulani into Hausaland, and later into Bornu. Some were herders who moved with their cattle through the year, some were semi-nomadic, and others lived permanently in towns.
features.evidence: Secondary sources, partly resting on oral tradition
features.location: Drawn through Katsina and Kano to Ngazargamu to stand for Hausaland and Bornu. People moved over a wide area and many generations, not along one route.
features.disputed: Where the Fulani came from is unclear. Language evidence points to Futa Toro in the Senegal valley, and one estimate, mainly from oral tradition, has migrants leaving it for the east between the 11th and 14th centuries.

features.name: Edo (Benin City)
features.reach_note: Rough. Benin's influence reached Lagos, about 250 km to the west, by about the mid-1500s, while the Niger, about 130 km to the east, seems to have been the limit of its rule. A circle cannot show that shape, so the halo only says that influence faded with distance.
features.what: Capital of the Kingdom of Benin, ruled by the Oba. Ewuare came to power in 1440 and expanded the former city-state.

features.name: Arochukwu
features.label: left
features.what: Centre of the Aro Confederacy and home of the Ibini Ukpabi oracle, with the Aro king and a central council.
features.location: Today's town of the same name.

features.name: Onitsha
features.what: A town on the Niger with kings called the Obi.
features.location: Today's town of the same name.
features.disputed: Onitsha's founding is dated to between 1630 and 1680 by one source, and to the 16th century by others.

features.name: Oguta
features.label: left
features.what: A monarchy on Oguta Lake that traded with the Aro; enslaved people were sold at a market there.
features.location: Today's town on the eastern bank of Oguta Lake.

features.name: Bonny
features.what: A port kingdom and one of the main trading towns of the coast. Enslaved people were sold there, and after Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 the port turned to palm oil, ivory and pepper.

features.name: Aro trade with Onitsha
features.what: The Aro traded with the Onitsha monarchy, and enslaved people were sold at Onitsha.

features.name: Aro trade with Oguta
features.what: The Aro traded with the Oguta monarchy, and enslaved people were sold at Oguta Lake.

features.name: Aro trade through Bonny
features.what: Bonny was one of the markets where enslaved people from the Aro trade were sold.

features.name: Igbo communities
features.reach_note: The dotted field is centred roughly on Igboland east of the Niger. It is a pattern, not a map of villages, and its edge is not a border.
features.what: Most Igbo communities were run by assemblies and councils of elders, built on patrilineages called umunna, and many towns were also partly governed by the Ozo title society.

features.name: Sokoto
features.what: Founded as a military camp in 1809, and the seat of the caliph, the Amir al-Mu'minin.

features.name: Gwandu
features.label: left
features.what: A co-capital of the caliphate, from which its emirs oversaw the western and southern lands. Other towns served as the western capital in some years.

features.name: Katsina
features.what: The emirate set up in Katsina after the jihad.

features.name: Kano
features.what: The emirate set up after jihad forces captured Kano in 1807.

features.name: Zaria
features.what: Zaria, capital of Zazzau, was captured by the Fulani in 1805 during the jihad.

features.name: Katsina's allegiance to Sokoto
features.what: Katsina's emir recognised the caliph at Sokoto as overlord, and travelled each year to pledge allegiance and bring tribute.

features.name: Kano's allegiance to Sokoto
features.what: Kano's emir recognised the caliph at Sokoto as overlord, and travelled each year to pledge allegiance and bring tribute.

features.name: Zazzau's allegiance to Sokoto
features.what: Zazzau's emir recognised the caliph at Sokoto as overlord, and travelled each year to pledge allegiance and bring tribute.

features.name: British campaign from Zaria to Kano and Sokoto
features.what: British forces took Zaria in 1901. A force under Colonel Thomas Morland left Zaria at the end of January 1903 and took Kano on 3 February. British forces under Kemball and Morland then took Sokoto after a battle on 15 March.
features.location: Straight lines join the towns in the order they were taken. The columns' routes are not shown, and the line from Kano to Sokoto stands for the British advance, not one column's march.
features.disputed: One source dates the battle for Sokoto to 15 March 1903; another says the caliphate's council conceded to Lugard's demands on 13 March.

scenes.title: Trade: salt across the Sahara
scenes.text: Trade is drawn as a dotted route with the goods travelling along it. Caravans carried rock salt south from Bilma, in the Kawar oases, to the savanna north of Lake Chad, where Kanem's heartland lay. In return, slaves and ivory went north. This was the shortest crossing of the Sahara, on the road from Tripoli by way of Murzuk. Regular caravan routes across the desert grew from the 7th and 8th centuries. Around 1380 Kanem's rulers lost their capital and moved west across the lake to Bornu.

scenes.title: City-states: the walled towns of the Hausa
scenes.text: A city-state is drawn as a walled town with its own name. The Hausa states were separate kingdoms around fortified capitals, never one kingdom, so no shared border is drawn. By the 15th century Kano and Katsina were trading centres that competed with Bornu and Mali. A thin line joins two places only where tribute or an alliance is documented, with the arrow pointing to the overlord: Kano paid tribute to Bornu. Rano is left off because Kano had conquered it earlier, and Gobir, Zazzau and Biram wait until the sites of their 15th-century capitals are checked.

scenes.title: Migration: Fulani into Hausaland and Bornu
scenes.text: Migration is drawn as a soft band of drifting dots with no arrowhead, because people moved over generations rather than marching on a target. By the 15th century there was a steady flow of Fulani into Hausaland, and later into Bornu. Some were herders who moved with their cattle through the year, and others settled in towns, so the band runs through the Hausa towns instead of forming a country of its own. Where the Fulani came from is unclear, so the band fades out at its western end.

scenes.title: A kingdom: Benin
scenes.text: A kingdom is drawn as its capital with a soft halo of influence that fades with distance, never as a hard border. In 1440 Ewuare came to power at Edo, today's Benin City, and expanded what had been a city-state. From the mid-15th century Benin's armies pushed west into eastern Yorubaland, and its influence reached Lagos by about the mid-1500s. The Niger seems to have been the eastern limit of its rule. The badge is the leopard, one of the principal symbols of the Oba in Benin art. It is drawn as a royal symbol, not a flag, because no flag of the kingdom is documented.

scenes.title: A network: the Aro
scenes.text: A network is drawn as threads from its centre, with no area filled in, because the Aro did not rule a territory. From Arochukwu, home of the Ibini Ukpabi oracle, the Aro traded with the monarchies of Onitsha and Oguta, among others. Enslaved people were sold at markets including Oguta Lake, Onitsha and Bonny, and the confederacy's economy rested mainly on enslaved people and palm oil. Neighbouring groups such as the Ohafia, Edda and Abam fought as its allies. British forces took Arochukwu on 28 December 1901, and the confederacy collapsed by early 1902.

scenes.title: Self-governing communities: Igbo towns and villages
scenes.text: Self-governing communities are drawn as a field of small dots with no capital and no edge. Most Igbo communities were run by assemblies and councils of elders, built on patrilineages called umunna, and many towns were also partly governed by the Ozo title society. There was no single Igbo kingdom, so none is drawn. A few places did have kings: Onitsha's were called the Obi, and Nri and Arochukwu had priest-kings.

scenes.title: A caliphate of emirates: Sokoto
scenes.text: A caliphate is drawn as the caliph's seat with a line from each emirate, showing allegiance rather than one border. The jihad that began in 1804 brought the Hausa states under new emirates: Zaria was captured in 1805 and Kano in 1807. Sokoto was founded as a military camp in 1809 and became the caliph's seat, and Gwandu became a co-capital from which the western and southern lands were overseen. Each emir was appointed by the caliph and governed with wide self-rule, travelling every year to pledge allegiance and bring tribute in crops, cowries and slaves.

scenes.title: Claimed on paper: the protectorates of 1900
scenes.text: A claim on paper is drawn as hatching, and it turns solid only where occupation is documented. On 1 January 1900 the Royal Niger Company handed its territories to the British government for £865,000, and with the Niger Coast Protectorate they became the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria. On paper, Sokoto, Kano and Zaria were now inside a British protectorate. On the ground, the caliph and the emirs still governed them.

scenes.title: A campaign: Zaria, Kano and Sokoto taken
scenes.text: A military campaign is drawn as a hard arrow with a pulse at each dated stop. As each town is taken, its hatching turns solid. British forces took Zaria in 1901. A force under Colonel Thomas Morland left Zaria at the end of January 1903 and took Kano on 3 February after heavy fighting. In March British forces reached Sokoto, which fell after a battle on 15 March. Caliph Attahiru I left the city, and was killed later in 1903.
scenes.disputed: Attahiru I's death is dated to June 1903 in one source and to the Battle of Burmi on 27 July 1903 in others.
